title: Knee Arthritis Exercises: What to Do and What to Avoid
note: Original version clinically reviewed by Louis Maxwell, 6 February 2026. Enhanced edition prepared 16 November 2026: editorial changes only. The revised wording has not yet had a fresh clinical review.
html:
Quick answer: Knee arthritis exercises can include gentle knee movement, muscle strengthening, walking, cycling and suitable water-based activity. Start gently, stay within a comfortable range and build up gradually. Avoid forcing painful movements or pushing through sharp, severe or unusual pain.

Why exercise matters for a painful knee

When a knee hurts, moving less can feel like the safest option, and rest certainly has its place on difficult days. But avoiding movement over long periods makes maintaining muscle strength and everyday mobility harder. For osteoarthritis, NICE recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to the individual, including local muscle strengthening and general aerobic fitness. Exercise does not cure or reverse knee arthritis.

The main options

  • Gentle mobility: knee bending and straightening to maintain comfortable movement.
  • Strengthening: controlled thigh and leg exercises to support the muscles around the knee.
  • Aerobic activity: walking or cycling to support fitness and stamina.
  • Water exercise: swimming or aqua exercise with support from the water.
  • Seated exercise: chair-based knee and ankle movements when standing is difficult.
  • Balance activity: supported exercises that may help stability and confidence.

Gentle knee movements and strengthening

While sitting securely in a stable chair, some people can slowly straighten one knee towards a comfortable position and then lower the foot again. Keep the movement controlled, and do not force the knee completely straight if that is painful or difficult. A smaller comfortable movement beats a forced bigger one.

Strengthening the muscles that support and move the knee is an important part of exercising with knee osteoarthritis, and it does not mean heavy weights. Depending on your ability and professional advice, it might involve controlled seated movements, light resistance, resistance bands, adapted standing exercises, body-weight exercises or water resistance.

Walking and cycling

Walking is a practical form of activity for many people, but the right amount varies. Instead of chasing a distance or step target, consider what your knee can currently manage: a shorter route, a comfortable pace, level ground and planned breaks. You do not have to walk until your knee forces you to stop; turning around earlier is part of pacing, not a defeat.

Cycling allows repeated knee movement without the same impact as running. Begin gently, avoid heavy resistance, and pay attention to bike setup. If cycling repeatedly aggravates your knee, stop and discuss technique or setup with a physiotherapist.

Water-based and seated exercise

Swimming and suitable water-based exercise are useful because the water supports your body. Gentle swimming, walking in shallow water, an appropriate aqua class or comfortable knee movements in water all count. Take care entering and leaving the pool if knee pain, weakness or balance difficulties affect your stability.

Chair-based exercise is a practical option when prolonged standing is difficult: gentle knee bending, comfortable knee straightening, ankle movements, upper-body movement and adapted strengthening from a stable chair on a secure surface.

What about squats and stairs?

There is no universal rule that everyone with knee arthritis must do or avoid squats. A squat places different demands on the knee depending on depth, technique, strength, balance, symptoms and resistance. Some people tolerate a shallow or supported version; others find squatting uncomfortable. Do not force a deep squat simply because it appears on an exercise programme.

Stairs are part of daily life and can be demanding with painful knees. Take your time, use a handrail where available, avoid rushing, and reduce unnecessary trips when symptoms are worse. If stairs become increasingly difficult or unsafe, discuss it with a healthcare professional.

What to avoid

  • Pushing through sharp or severe pain. Pain is not proof that an exercise is working.
  • Suddenly increasing activity. Build up gradually.
  • Forcing the knee through its range. Stay within what is comfortable.
  • Repeating an activity that significantly worsens symptoms. It may need modifying.
  • Assuming high-impact exercise is essential. Whether it is suitable depends on your circumstances.
  • Comparing your programme with someone else's. Symptoms, strength and mobility vary.

Safety first

"No pain, no gain" is not an appropriate approach to exercising with arthritis. A successful exercise plan is not the hardest one; it is one you can approach safely and realistically.

Flare days, and how much pain is too much

A more painful day may need a different approach: a shorter session, reduced resistance, gentler movements, additional breaks or a rest from an activity that clearly aggravates symptoms. Adapting your exercise does not mean giving up.

There is no single pain rule that applies to everyone. Some people notice temporary discomfort when starting a new activity, but exercise should not involve forcing yourself through significant pain. Stop or modify if pain becomes sharp, severe or unusual, and seek professional advice if exercise repeatedly causes considerable worsening, swelling or difficulty using the knee afterwards.

When knee pain should be checked

Speak to your GP if knee pain is new, persistent, worsening or significantly affecting everyday life, and do not automatically assume every new knee symptom is caused by arthritis. Physiotherapy can be particularly useful if you are uncertain about exercising a painful knee, your knee feels unstable, mobility has changed, you use a walking aid, or exercises repeatedly aggravate symptoms.

Seek urgent medical advice if your knee or another joint becomes severely painful, hot, red or significantly swollen, particularly if you feel unwell or have a high temperature. Seek emergency help after a serious injury if the knee has changed shape or you cannot put weight on it, and for chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, sudden weakness or numbness, or loss of bladder or bowel control.

Key takeaways

  • Adapt knee exercises to your symptoms and ability; the right amount varies between people.
  • Gentle movement maintains mobility; strengthening supports the muscles that move the knee.
  • Walking, cycling, water-based and seated exercise are all realistic options.
  • Start gently, increase gradually, rest when needed, and stop if pain becomes sharp, severe or unusual.
  • Exercise supports function but does not cure or reverse knee arthritis.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best exercise for knee arthritis?

There is no single best exercise for everyone. Gentle mobility, appropriate strengthening, walking, cycling and water-based activity may all be useful depending on your symptoms and ability.

Are squats bad for knee arthritis?

Not necessarily. Some people tolerate modified or shallow squats, while others find them uncomfortable. Technique, depth, strength and individual symptoms matter.

Is cycling good for arthritic knees?

Cycling may be suitable for some people. A stationary bike lets you control resistance and duration. Start gently and seek advice if cycling repeatedly aggravates symptoms.

Can exercise cure knee arthritis?

No. Exercise does not cure or reverse knee arthritis, but appropriately tailored exercise can support strength, mobility, fitness and everyday function.

A gentle next step

Living with knee arthritis does not mean choosing between doing nothing and pushing through pain. Start with manageable movement and gradually find the right balance. If you are unsure which knee exercises are appropriate for you, speak to your GP, physiotherapist or another appropriate healthcare professional, and explore practical arthritis information and support from Living With Arthritis.
